questions.prompt: What is the core distinction between a Business Requirements Document (BRD) and a Functional Requirements Document (FRD)?

options.text: BRD defines business objectives and what value is needed; FRD specifies how the system behaves to fulfill them
FRD is written only after production launch
BRD contains SQL table DDL exclusively
There is no difference; they are identical

questions.explanation: BRDs capture business goals, scope, and high-level needs; FRDs translate those into detailed system behaviors, rules, and validations.

rubric.label: Separates business intent from system behavior

questions.prompt: Which statement is an example of a measurable Non-Functional Requirement (NFR)?

options.text: The system should be fast and user-friendly
The checkout API must respond within 300ms at P95 under 500 concurrent users
Users can click the submit button

questions.explanation: Good NFRs are quantitative, testable, and specify operating conditions (latency percentile + load).

questions.prompt: During requirements elicitation, operational users describe a workaround they use every Friday that contradicts the written SOP. What should the System Analyst do?

options.text: Ignore the workaround and copy the old SOP verbatim
Document the real-world exception, validate why it exists with business owners, and design explicit handling in the FRD
Tell the users to stop doing their job
Leave it for developers to guess

questions.explanation: Shadowing reveals tacit business rules and exception paths that written SOPs often miss.

questions.prompt: Select ALL qualities of a well-written functional requirement (IEEE 29148 / INVEST).

options.text: Bundles five unrelated features into one paragraph

questions.explanation: Atomic, unambiguous, consistent, and traceable requirements prevent downstream rework in engineering and QA.

questions.prompt: In MoSCoW prioritization, what does the "Could-have" category signify?

options.text: Desirable enhancement included only if time and budget permit without impacting Must/Should items
Explicitly out of scope for this release

questions.explanation: Could-have items act as the primary scope buffer to protect Must-have delivery dates.

questions.prompt: Rewrite the vague stakeholder request "The invoice approval screen should notify finance quickly" into two concrete functional/non-functional requirements with clear acceptance criteria.
questions.explanation: Strong specs define the exact trigger event, recipient role, delivery channel, latency SLA, and failure fallback.

rubric.label: Translates vague intent into testable rules

questions.prompt: Which UML diagram is best suited for illustrating time-ordered message exchanges between a browser, API gateway, and payment provider?
questions.explanation: Sequence diagrams explicitly model lifelines, synchronous/asynchronous calls, and chronological message order.

rubric.label: Selects Sequence Diagram for temporal flows
Matches diagram type to modeling goal

questions.prompt: In a BPMN or UML Activity Diagram, what do "swimlanes" represent?

options.text: Ownership boundaries showing which actor, role, or system performs each activity

questions.explanation: Swimlanes clarify handoffs and accountability across roles or systems in an end-to-end process.

questions.prompt: When modeling an order lifecycle (Draft -> Submitted -> Approved -> Paid -> Refunded) with strict guard conditions, which UML diagram is most appropriate?
questions.explanation: State Machine diagrams capture valid states, triggering events, guard conditions, and disallowed transitions.

rubric.label: Models lifecycle rules via State Machine

questions.prompt: In a UML Use Case diagram, what does an `<<include>>` relationship between Use Case A and Use Case B indicate?

options.text: Use Case B is optional and rarely runs
Use Case A always invokes the behavior of Use Case B as a mandatory sub-step
Use Case B replaces Use Case A

questions.explanation: <<include>> models mandatory reused behavior (e.g., Authenticate), whereas <<extend>> models optional/conditional behavior.

questions.prompt: Select ALL elements that should appear in an accurate integration data-mapping specification.

options.text: Source and target field names with data types and lengths

questions.explanation: Complete field mappings eliminate silent truncation, timezone drift, and schema mismatch bugs.

questions.prompt: Describe the key lifelines, synchronous calls, and failure branch you would draw in a Sequence Diagram for a 3DS card payment confirmation flow.
questions.explanation: Include Customer, Checkout API, Payment Gateway, and Issuer Bank lifelines with an alt/else fragment for declined or timed-out challenges.

questions.prompt: What is the primary output of a structured Fit-Gap Analysis when evaluating a COTS/SaaS platform against current business processes?

options.text: A list of every employee's salary
A categorized matrix of Fits, Configuration Gaps, Customizations, and Process Workarounds with effort/risk ratings

questions.explanation: Fit-Gap analysis makes buy-vs-build and process-change trade-offs transparent before implementation.

rubric.label: Categorizes fits, configs, and custom gaps

questions.prompt: A legacy ERP stores customer tax IDs in a free-text 50-character field, while the new system enforces a strict 12-digit numeric format. What type of gap is this?

options.text: Data quality and schema validation gap requiring cleansing and migration rules

questions.explanation: Legacy-to-target schema mismatches require pre-migration profiling, cleansing rules, and exception handling.

questions.prompt: Before recommending a costly custom code extension to close a SaaS functional gap, what should a Lead System Analyst evaluate first?

options.text: Whether standard configuration or minor business process alignment can satisfy the underlying need
How to bypass vendor support warranties
Whether to hide the gap until UAT

questions.explanation: Customizations increase upgrade and maintenance costs; adopting standard capability where viable lowers total cost of ownership.

questions.prompt: Which technique establishes the baseline before performing a To-Be gap analysis?

options.text: Documenting the current As-Is state (processes, systems, pain points, and metrics)

questions.explanation: Without an accurate As-Is baseline, gaps, hidden integrations, and transition risks are easily missed.

questions.prompt: Your company is migrating from an on-prem payroll tool to a cloud HRIS that lacks a legacy multi-currency bonus export. Outline your gap closure recommendation options.
questions.explanation: Compare options: standard report + lightweight middleware transform, vendor roadmap wait, or custom integration — weighted by maintenance cost and compliance.

rubric.label: Weighs maintenance cost vs business value

questions.prompt: What is a "transition requirement" in BABOK terminology?

options.text: A temporary capability needed only to move from the current state to the future state (e.g., data migration, parallel run, training)

questions.explanation: Transition requirements are critical for safe cutover even though they are retired once migration succeeds.

questions.prompt: What is the purpose of a Requirements Traceability Matrix (RTM)?

options.text: Link every business requirement forward to design, test cases, and UAT sign-off (and backward to origin)

questions.explanation: An RTM ensures zero orphaned requirements and proves full test coverage prior to release sign-off.

questions.prompt: Who is primarily responsible for executing and signing off User Acceptance Testing (UAT)?

options.text: Business end-users / product owners validating real-world workflows against acceptance criteria

questions.explanation: UAT confirms fitness for business use by the actual business representatives who own the workflow.

rubric.label: Separates UAT from developer unit testing

questions.prompt: Which exit criteria should be met before formal UAT sign-off is granted?

options.text: 100% of planned UAT scenarios executed, 0 open S1/S2 defects, and documented workarounds/deferrals for any minor S3/S4 items
At least 10% of test cases run
Developers say it works on their laptop

questions.explanation: Objective UAT exit criteria prevent ambiguous go-live decisions and ensure critical defects are closed.

questions.prompt: Select ALL prerequisites that must be ready BEFORE UAT kickoff (UAT entry criteria).

options.text: System Integration Testing (SIT) completed with no S1/S2 blockers
Representative anonymized test data loaded in UAT environment
Approved UAT test scripts and defect-logging workflow
Unmerged feature branches still in development

questions.explanation: Starting UAT without stable SIT, realistic test data, and scripts wastes business-user time.

questions.prompt: During UAT, a tester reports a "defect" for a feature that was never in the approved FRD. How should the System Analyst classify it?

options.text: Change Request / Enhancement to be triaged against release scope

questions.explanation: Comparing against the baselined FRD distinguishes true defects (deviations from spec) from new scope requests.

rubric.label: Separates spec defects from scope changes

questions.prompt: Write 3 concise Given/When/Then UAT acceptance scenarios for a role-based discount approval workflow (discounts > 15% require manager approval).
questions.explanation: Cover boundary values: <= 15% auto-approved, > 15% routed to manager pending state, and manager rejection notification.
